"Gunbot Diplomacy: Blast Off" is a top-down shooter roguelite. The game's story revolves around you assembling and customizing a "Gunbot" to survive hordes of various enemies in a post-apocalyptic wasteland. The prologue allows you to try out two gunbots with a selection of weapons and modules. This is from the shovelware pushes at GrabTheGames and has a HUGE number of fake reviews all in Chinese that all arrived immediately at launch. No co-incidences here. What do you do in the game? Bady done "I can't believe it's not a GameMaker Studio asset flip" top down shooting. You customize your weapons using a unique upgrade grid and select from a variety of build-defining modules. You can choose to manually aim or let your gunbot's automated targeting handle the firing... but this really isn't worth playing, from garbage game design, garbage quality, garbage visuals, garbage fake reviews and of course, no content. This features really godawful pixelcrap "art" instead of real graphics. It's hard to say if this was because the developer didn't have the skill to do the job of creating 3D visuals, or couldn't afford to hire someone who does, but it also doesn't matter. What matters is that this looks much worse than most other games because of that decision, and that's a major deterrent to gamers. Games like Terraria and Stardew Valley succeeded [i]despite[/i] the bad graphics, not because of them. The developer chose not to do the job of a real game developer and create meaningful bespoke levels, narrative based gameplay progression and so on. Instead, they decided that "Procgen IS content!" and lazily tried to use procgen algorithms to create infinite, samey, repetitive, soulless levels, because that's a lot less work. As a result of this poor decision, the game gets tired and repetitive almost immediately. Developers must learn that procgen is a terrible substitute for creating real content. It should not be used as "ez-mode" for content creation, as the developer tried to do here. On pricing, this is "free" enough, at least you won't be expected to spend any more money after you download this, but just because something is free doesn't mean it's good, and the cost of a game is more than just financial, your time is valuable too. It's important to note that, despite this being such a low quality product, there's a number of positive reviews that all appeared immediately after the game launched, from suspiciously inactive Steam accounts that have reviewed almost no other games apart from this. Take the review score of this game with a grain of salt. Bearing in mind that free games don't add +1 to your game collector count, should you bother adding this to your library and downloading it? Nope. This isn't worth downloading. While this didn't cost me any money up front, I still feel ripped off.

Okay-ish demo of a game that copies a lot out of other auto-survival shooters like + Brotatos (best! + Coop!) + Deep Rock Survival (2nd best game, was primary "target of inspiration" for this game) + Vampire Survivor (is kinda boring) Unique is the setup of the hexagon abilitys. guns and effects react with the tiles around them. So in theory there could be some interesting tinkering possible. Yet, the demo didn't really feel that deep in the development. - The "coins" you need to pick up are hard to see. - The character animations are low quality (2D layer gets "turned" if enemies change direction) - menue music had to be turned off - Unlock grind to prolong gaming experiments. Modern "Rogue-Like" approach, thats not much fun. - Very uncool: Add title to steam wishlist, so you can get the next Character. Cheap sales method. This game looks like a quick release to get some money. Or had an impatient publisher. It's not enough to be considered good. Could be in a way good, but signs are there. So wouldn't bet on it. Let's wait and see how people will rate it in the end. For me right now it has no recommendation. But will follow it and change my opinion. I support Indy Devs but not money grabs. The question is: Which one is it? :-/

A top-down shooting experience built around constant chaos: screens packed with projectiles, enemies pouring in without pause, and a pace that barely allows the player to breathe. From the very first moments, it becomes clear that the game’s goal is not precision or clean readability, but rather to immerse the player in an unbroken storm of stimuli. That approach comes at a cost. The accumulation of flashes, explosions, particles, and luminous trails often turns many situations into visual noise that is hard to parse. It is not always easy to tell what is actually happening, where the real danger is coming from, or which escape route is viable. The game conveys intensity, but frequently does so at the expense of clarity—something especially problematic in a genre where spatial awareness and anticipation are essential. Mechanically, the title does not stray far from what other survival shooters already offer: constant movement, dodging, enduring ever-denser waves. Where it does introduce a personal touch is in its system of weapons and modules. The ability to expand, combine, and transform the robot’s equipment adds a layer of interest that encourages experimentation with different configurations. This is where its most distinctive trait emerges: the feeling of “building” your own way of playing from run to run. Beyond that system, however, the experience tends to feel familiar. Matches follow a recognizable pattern, and once the initial impact wears off, the loop reveals itself as predictable. Progression relies heavily on randomness, meaning some sessions shine while others feel flat, with little room for the player to compensate. The end result is a functional game—occasionally entertaining—but one that does not quite justify an immediate purchase if what you seek are new sensations or a strong identity. It has an interesting idea at its core—the modular evolution of weaponry—but that idea is wrapped in an overly invasive presentation and a structure that does not distance itself enough from what is already known. For now, it feels more like a competent curiosity within the genre than an essential experience. ----------------------------------------------------------------- Juego/experiencia de disparos vista desde arriba que se apoya en el caos constante: pantallas llenas de proyectiles, enemigos que brotan sin descanso y un ritmo que apenas concede respiro. Desde el primer minuto queda claro que su intención no es la precisión ni la lectura limpia del entorno, sino sumergir al jugador en una tormenta continua de estímulos. Ese enfoque tiene un coste. La acumulación de destellos, explosiones, partículas y trazas luminosas acaba convirtiendo muchas situaciones en un ruido visual difícil de descifrar. No siempre es sencillo distinguir qué está ocurriendo, por dónde llega el peligro real o cuál es la mejor ruta de escape. El juego transmite intensidad, pero a menudo lo hace sacrificando claridad, algo especialmente problemático en un género donde la percepción espacial y la anticipación son claves. En lo mecánico, el título no se aleja demasiado de lo que ya ofrecen otros shooters de supervivencia: moverse sin parar, esquivar, resistir oleadas cada vez más densas. Donde sí introduce un matiz propio es en el sistema de armas y módulos. La posibilidad de ampliar, combinar y transformar el equipamiento del robot añade una capa de interés que invita a experimentar con configuraciones distintas. Es ahí donde aparece su rasgo más personal: la sensación de “construir” tu forma de jugar partida a partida. Sin embargo, más allá de ese sistema, la experiencia tiende a sentirse familiar. Las partidas siguen un patrón reconocible y, una vez superado el impacto inicial, el bucle se revela como predecible. La progresión depende en buena medida del azar, lo que provoca que algunas sesiones brillen y otras se sientan planas sin que el jugador tenga demasiado margen para corregirlo. El resultado es un juego funcional, incluso entretenido por momentos, pero que no termina de justificar una compra inmediata si se buscan sensaciones nuevas o una identidad fuerte. Tiene una idea interesante en su núcleo —la evolución modular del armamento—, pero queda envuelta en una presentación demasiado invasiva y en una estructura que no se desmarca lo suficiente de lo ya conocido. Hoy por hoy, se percibe más como una curiosidad competente dentro del género que como una propuesta imprescindible.
